clue.text: Run faster in striking football kit

parts.note: workers who are striking are out, on strike
a team's strip is its football kit

explanation.surface: A footballer sprints away while wearing the team's striking new kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' looks like an adjective for eye-catching kit, but 'in striking' means on strike, OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: To outrun someone is to leave them behind, a straightforward synonym for running faster.

clue.text: Go underground, we're told, to park in London

indicators.note: signals that the word for going underground is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to go underground is to hide away

explanation.surface: Advice to slip away into the London Underground near a park.
explanation.walkthrough: Hyde Park is the large royal park in central London.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyde Park is a famous royal park in central London, so the name defines it directly.

clue.text: Animal has no end of courage in a melee

indicators.note: a melee is a confused scramble, so the remaining letters are jumbled
the final letter of the word courage is dropped

explanation.surface: A beast loses its nerve when caught up in a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end of' drops the last E of COURAGE, leaving COURAG, which 'in a melee' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: The cougar, or puma, is a large wild cat of the Americas: an example of an animal.

clue.text: Logical businessman gets money from tenants

parts.note: business split off gives CO, the abbreviation for company
the man in the word gives HE, the pronoun for a man
tenants pay rent to their landlord

explanation.surface: A sensible landlord collects the rent from his tenants.
explanation.walkthrough: The single word 'businessman' is split into two pieces, an abbreviation for a firm and a pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: A coherent argument hangs together consistently, which is what makes it logical.

clue.text: Flora vetoing tea break

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone called Flora refuses to allow a tea break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flora' reads as a woman's name but means plant life.
explanation.definitionFit: Flora is the plant life of a region, collectively its vegetation.

clue.text: Earned aggravation, when closed

indicators.note: trouble stirred up, so the letters of earned are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone got only irritation for their trouble once the shop shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'closed' here means drew close, approached, not shut.
explanation.definitionFit: To close on something is to get nearer to it, so closed means approached.

clue.text: Energetic group, one out to make mischief

parts.note: someone energetic is busy, always on the go
a body is an organised group of people

explanation.surface: A lively gang includes one member who stirs up trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A meddler who pries into others' affairs often causes trouble, so is out to make mischief.

clue.text: A money changer, who had a farm

indicators.note: a changer alters things, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bureau de change worker who once owned a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'money changer' reads as one phrase, but 'changer' is the anagram signal for A MONEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a yeoman was a freeholding farmer who cultivated his own land.

clue.text: Beginner in a key role

parts.note: something that begins proceedings, and also a tool doing the job of a key, as a tin or bottle device does

explanation.surface: A novice actor lands an important part.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the batsman who starts the innings is also called this.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the first item or player in a sequence, and also a device that unlocks or unseals like a key.

clue.text: In French is it spelt without the S? Yes

definitions.text: In French is it spelt without the S? Yes

parts.words: In French is it spelt without the S? Yes
parts.note: modern French writes île for an island, dropping the S of the older spelling, so the English word lacks only that change

explanation.surface: A spelling question about French answered briskly.
explanation.walkthrough: The French île once had an S, which survives in the English form.
explanation.definitionFit: A small island is spelt île in French, without the S the English word keeps.

clue.text: Third party?

parts.note: not an insurance term but the unwanted extra person with a courting couple

explanation.walkthrough: 'Third party' suggests insurance or law; to play this fruit is British slang for being the awkward extra with a couple.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'to play gooseberry' means tagging along as an unwanted chaperone with lovers.

clue.text: He's happy to give people his address

definitions.text: He's happy to give people his address

parts.words: He's happy to give people his address
parts.note: not a home address freely shared, but a speech delivered to an audience

explanation.surface: A friendly man readily tells others where he lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'address' means a formal speech, not a place of residence.
explanation.definitionFit: A public speaker delights in delivering speeches, or addresses, to an audience.

clue.text: Opportunity for murder? Nothing else to do

definitions.meaning: read literally, a moment suited to slaying someone
the idiom for spare hours with nothing to fill them

explanation.surface: A bored killer finds the perfect chance to strike.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means having spare hours on one's hands, and literally a moment for slaying.

clue.text: City set within a river

indicators.note: one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland
laid, as a table is laid or set

explanation.surface: A town built beside a waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dee is a British river, often used in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Adelaide is the capital of South Australia, a major Australian city.

clue.text: Lock oil?

parts.note: not lubricant for a door lock but grease for a lock of hair

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' suggests a door or canal, but here it is a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: This perfumed hair grease is used to slick down locks of hair.

clue.text: Guard the stupid girl

indicators.note: something stupid is muddled, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: An instruction to protect a foolish young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A female child is a girl relative to her parents, so girl stands for her.

clue.text: Fighting prevalent on street

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece goes on after the other

parts.note: something rife is widespread or prevalent

explanation.surface: Violence is common in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: Strife means conflict or bitter disagreement, so it amounts to fighting.

clue.text: Sally in deep trouble, turned out

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other
the letters of deep are troubled, stirred into a new order

parts.note: a sally is a witty remark, a quip

explanation.surface: A woman named Sally is in serious difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges the letters of 'deep' into EPED, and 'in' places the witticism inside. 'Sally' looks like a name but means a witty remark.
explanation.definitionFit: To be well turned out is to be dressed or fitted out, so turned out means kitted up.

clue.text: A dandy, too

parts.note: a swell is a dated word for a fashionable dandy

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in addition, also, so it is a synonym for too.

clue.text: Wild Etruscan horsemen

indicators.note: wild suggests disorder, so the letters of Etruscan run amok

explanation.surface: Ancient Italian riders charging fiercely.
explanation.definitionFit: These mythical creatures are half man and half horse, hence horsemen in a literal sense.

clue.text: An extremely self-conscious person

parts.note: not someone shy but someone overly conscious of the self, utterly self-centred

explanation.surface: Someone painfully shy and awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'self-conscious' usually means embarrassed; taken literally it means always thinking about oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-centred person thinks constantly of himself, being conscious above all of his own interests.

clue.text: Washday queue?

parts.note: a queue is a row of people, and on washday the washing goes on the clothes line, raised up

explanation.walkthrough: A queue is a line-up; on washday you put up the washing line.
explanation.definitionFit: A row of people waiting is a line-up, and on laundry day the clothes line goes up.

clue.text: What is wrong in record being beaten?

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a log is a written record, as a ship's log
a sin is something morally wrong

explanation.surface: A query about what is amiss in a defeated team's record.
explanation.definitionFit: A side being beaten in a match is currently on the wrong end of the score.

clue.text: Tasks for students need short week's revision

indicators.note: revising alters the text, so these letters are reorganised

explanation.surface: Pupils get assignments to revise in a shortened week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revision' looks like study for exams but signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: These printed exercise pages set work for pupils, so they are tasks for students.

clue.text: Not a fully grown creature, whichever way you look at it

definitions.text: Not a fully grown creature, whichever way you look at it

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: looking at it the other way round means reading the letters from the end back to the start

parts.note: governed by the opening 'Not', a creature short of fully grown is a young dog, a pup

explanation.surface: An immature animal that looks immature from any angle.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue works twice: 'a' plus a young dog, turned round, gives the insect stage, and both a pup and that insect stage are not fully grown. The answer also reads the same either way round.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the insect stage between larva and adult, so the creature is not yet fully developed.

clue.text: Licence is almost out of date

indicators.note: the final letter of the word is left off

parts.note: ...é means old-fashioned, out of date

explanation.surface: A permit that has nearly expired.
explanation.definitionFit: A permit allowing entry or travel is a pass, a form of licence.

clue.text: Wagnerian heroine that is at heart betrayed

indicators.note: one piece sits in the middle of the other

parts.note: IE is the abbreviation of id est, that is
to sell someone out is to betray them, so sold means betrayed

explanation.surface: An opera heroine whose love is betrayed.
explanation.walkthrough: Wagner's opera Tristan und Isolde tells of her doomed love.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the Irish princess heroine of Wagner's opera of tragic love with Tristan.

clue.text: He painted a country view with river

parts.note: a land is a country or nation
to view is to see

explanation.surface: An artist depicted a rural landscape with a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Edwin Landseer was a Victorian painter famous for animal pictures and the Trafalgar Square lions.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwin Landseer was a celebrated nineteenth-century English painter, so he is one who painted.
